literature.headline_zh: 人腺病毒本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期人腺病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 从该患者的外周血中总共分离了2710个B细胞,并通过整合scRNA-seq和scVDJ-seq技术全面分析了B细胞亚群和B细胞受体(BCR)库的特征。 [10.3390/ijms27208952]
在 HAdV-2 存在的情况下,DPPG 脂质体的相变温度 (Tm) 增加约 11 °C,而病毒颗粒本身没有观察到可检测到的结构变化。 [10.1007/s10895-026-04962-7]

基因组和系统发育分析证实,HAdV-3-TZ01 属于 B 种内的 HAdV-3,并表现出与当代流行的 HAdV-3 毒株高度保守的基因组骨架。功能表征揭示了病毒 基因组 在人呼吸道上皮细胞和多种上皮源性肿瘤细胞系中的强大复制。病毒 基因组 水平在 H3122、BEAS-2B 和 A549 细胞中迅速增加,而在鼠 L929 细胞中复制受到显着限制。HAdV-3-TZ01 还在低多重性条件下在几种人类肿瘤细胞系中显示出活跃的病毒 基因组 复制。 [PMCID:PMC13642665]
SEM 成像显示,在 NTP 暴露后,纸张没有明显的形态变化,毛绒织物中有轻微的纤维卷曲,泡沫橡胶没有结构损坏。XPS 分析表明表面轻度氧化,没有显着的结构变化。 [PMCID:PMC13646080]
没有已发表的证据表明这些设备会传播威胁视力的感染,或者与较低水平的消毒方法相比,HLD 可以减少感染 传播。许多使用化学 HLD 的受访者报告了不良反应,包括眼表化学毒性和设备损坏。 [10.1016/j.ophtha.2026.10.008]

In the presence of HAdV-2, the phase transition temperature (Tm) of DPPG liposomes increased by approximately 11 °C, while no detectable structural changes were observed in the viral particle itself. [10.1007/s10895-026-04962-7]

Genomic and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that HAdV-3-TZ01 belonged to HAdV-3 within species B and exhibited a genomic backbone highly conserved with contemporary circulating HAdV-3 strains. [PMCID:PMC13642665]

SEM imaging showed no substantial morphological alterations in paper after NTP exposure, minor fiber coiling in plush fabric, and no structural damage in foam rubber. XPS analysis indicated mild surface oxidation without significant structural changes. [PMCID:PMC13646080]

No published evidence was found that these devices transmit sight-threatening infections or that HLD reduces infection transmission compared with lower-level disinfection methods. papers.title: Intrinsic Fluorescence as a Probe of Structural Dynamics and Interactions of Human Adenovirus with Surfactants and Liposomes
papers.abstract: In this work, the intrinsic fluorescence of Human Adenovirus serotype 2 (HAdV-2), arising from tryptophan (Trp) and tyrosine (Tyr) residues present in viral proteins, was used to monitor structural changes in the three-dimensional organization of the viral particle as a function of the inactivation method employed (UV irradiation or paraformaldehyde (PFA) treatment), temperature, and the presence of negatively and positively charged surfactants. Steady-state fluorescence anisotropy was used to investigate the interaction between HAdV-2 and zwitterionic or negatively charged liposomes by monitoring both the extrinsic fluorescent probe 1,6-diphenyl-1,3,5-hexatriene (DPH) inserted into the lipid bilayer and the intrinsic anisotropy of Trp residues from viral proteins. Tyr fluorescence emission proved to be more sensitive to temperature variations, whereas Trp emission was more strongly affected in samples inactivated with PFA. In the presence of surfactants, stronger interactions were observed with negatively charged micelles, resulting in enhanced Tyr fluorescence and quenched Trp fluorescence. The most pronounced effect was observed for the interaction between HAdV-2 and negatively charged 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol), sodium salt (DPPG) liposomes. In the presence of viral particles, the phase transition temperature (Tm) of DPPG liposomes increased by approximately 11 °C, while no detectable structural changes were observed in the three-dimensional organization of the viral particle itself. Overall, these results highlight intrinsic fluorescence as a valuable approach for probing the structural organization of HAdV-2 under different environmental and interfacial conditions.

papers.title_zh: 固有荧光作为结构动力学和 人腺病毒 与表面活性剂和脂质体相互作用的探针
papers.source_body_en: In this work, the intrinsic fluorescence of Human Adenovirus serotype 2 (HAdV-2), arising from tryptophan (Trp) and tyrosine (Tyr) residues present in viral proteins, was used to monitor structural changes in the three-dimensional organization of the viral particle as a function of the inactivation method employed (UV irradiation or paraformaldehyde (PFA) treatment), temperature, and the presence of negatively and positively charged surfactants. Steady-state fluorescence anisotropy was used to investigate the interaction between HAdV-2 and zwitterionic or negatively charged liposomes by monitoring both the extrinsic fluorescent probe 1,6-diphenyl-1,3,5-hexatriene (DPH) inserted into the lipid bilayer and the intrinsic anisotropy of Trp residues from viral proteins. Tyr fluorescence emission proved to be more sensitive to temperature variations, whereas Trp emission was more strongly affected in samples inactivated with PFA. In the presence of surfactants, stronger interactions were observed with negatively charged micelles, resulting in enhanced Tyr fluorescence and quenched Trp fluorescence. The most pronounced effect was observed for the interaction between HAdV-2 and negatively charged 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1'-rac-glycerol), sodium salt (DPPG) liposomes. In the presence of viral particles, the phase transition temperature (Tm) of DPPG liposomes increased by approximately 11 °C, while no detectable structural changes were observed in the three-dimensional organization of the viral particle itself. Overall, these results highlight intrinsic fluorescence as a valuable approach for probing the structural organization of HAdV-2 under different environmental and interfacial conditions.
papers.abstract_zh: 在这项工作中,人腺病毒 血清型 2 (HAdV-2) 的固有荧光由病毒蛋白中存在的色氨酸 (Trp) 和酪氨酸 (Tyr) 残基产生,用于监测病毒颗粒三维组织的结构变化,作为所采用的灭活方法(紫外线照射或多聚甲醛 (PFA) 治疗)、温度以及负电荷和正电荷的存在的函数。表面活性剂。稳态荧光各向异性用于通过监测插入脂质双层的外在荧光探针 1,6-二苯基-1,3,5-己三烯 (DPH) 和病毒蛋白色氨酸残基的内在各向异性来研究 HAdV-2 与两性离子或带负电荷的脂质体之间的相互作用。Tyr 荧光发射被证明对温度变化更敏感,而 Trp 发射在用 PFA 灭活的样品中受到更强烈的影响。在存在表面活性剂的情况下,观察到与带负电荷的胶束有更强的相互作用,导致 Tyr 荧光增强并猝灭 Trp 荧光。观察到 HAdV-2 和带负电的 1,2-二棕榈酰-sn-甘油-3-磷酸-(1'-rac-甘油)钠盐 (DPPG) 脂质体之间的相互作用最显着。在病毒颗粒存在的情况下,DPPG脂质体的相变温度(Tm)增加了约11°C,而病毒颗粒本身的三维组织中没有观察到可检测到的结构变化。总的来说,这些结果强调了内在荧光是在不同环境和界面条件下探测 HAdV-2 结构组织的一种有价值的方法。

papers.title: Single-Cell BCR and Transcriptome Analysis Revealed Potent Neutralizing Antibodies in Response to HAdV-4 Infection
papers.abstract: Human adenovirus type 4 (HAdV-4) is a predominant serotype causing acute respiratory infections, for which no antibody drugs have been clinically approved to date, resulting in an urgent unmet medical need. This study aimed to identify highly potent neutralizing antibodies by dissecting the B cell immune response after infection, thereby laying a foundation for vaccine design and antiviral therapy. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from a convalescent patient who exhibited the most robust neutralizing antibody titers among 16 HAdV-4 convalescent volunteers. A total of 2710 B cells were isolated from the peripheral blood of this patient, and the characteristics of B cell subsets and B cell receptor (BCR) repertoires were comprehensively analyzed by integrating scRNA-seq and scVDJ-seq technologies. Candidate antibodies were subsequently selected for a series of functional and mechanistic validations based on the characteristics of BCRs and origination. Transcriptomic profiling classified memory B cells into three functionally heterogeneous subpopulations designated as MB sub1, sub2 and sub3. Combined with the characteristics of BCR, 92 selected antibodies from sub2 and sub3 were synthesized for further functional validation. Three potent neutralizing antibodies were successfully identified, among which 1QH7 demonstrated potentially potent virus neutralization capability in vitro and conferred robust in vivo protection in the Stat1-deficient mouse model. We further employed AlphaFold 3 to predict the complex structure of 1QH7 with the HAdV-4 Hexon protein and validated the key binding residues through site-directed mutagenesis. Additionally, the study elucidated the viral neutralization mechanism mediated by TRIM21. We established an efficient antibody screening strategy based on integration of scRNA-seq and scVDJ-seq and isolated a potent neutralizing antibody, 1QH7. This study lays a solid foundation for the rapid pathogen-bait-free, cell subset-guided screening antibody route for novel emerging infectious disease outbreaks.

papers.full_text: IntroductionHuman adenovirus type 3 (HAdV-3) is a major adenovirus type associated with respiratory infections in China. Despite its clinical importance, the biological characteristics and potential biomedical applications of contemporary circulating HAdV-3 strains remain incompletely understood. Naturally occurring species B adenoviruses also remain relatively underexplored as potential starting backbones for oncolytic virotherapy. This study aimed to characterize a contemporary clinical HAdV-3 isolate and evaluate its viral genome amplification, apoptosis induction, and antitumor activity.MethodsA clinical HAdV-3 isolate, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, was recovered from a throat swab specimen from a patient with adenovirus-associated respiratory disease. Viral identity and genomic characteristics were determined using multiplex PCR, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and recombination analysis. Viral genome amplification kinetics were evaluated in human respiratory-related and tumor-derived cell lines and a murine cell line by quantitative PCR. Comparative apoptosis induction by HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 was assessed in 293F cells infected at a low multiplicity of infection using Annexin V/PI flow cytometry. Antitumor activity was evaluated following repeated intratumoral administration of HAdV-3-TZ01 in an A549-luciferase xenograft model in BALB/c-nu nude mice, with tumor growth and bioluminescence monitored longitudinally.ResultsGenomic and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that HAdV-3-TZ01 belonged to HAdV-3 within species B and exhibited a genomic backbone highly conserved with contemporary circulating HAdV-3 strains. A short putative HAdV-7-derived recombinant fragment was identified. HAdV-3-TZ01 showed efficient viral genome amplification in multiple human respiratory-related cell lines, including A549, H3122, BEAS-2B, MRC-5, and HEK293FT cells, whereas genome amplification was markedly restricted in murine L929 cells. HAdV-3-TZ01 induced a significantly higher proportion of late apoptotic cells than HAdV-5 in 293F cells under low-multiplicity infection conditions, although the absolute increase in total apoptosis was modest. In the A549-luciferase xenograft model, intratumoral administration of HAdV-3-TZ01 significantly suppressed tumor progression. By day 43, mean tumor volume was reduced by approximately 54% and tumor-associated bioluminescence by approximately 50% compared with mock-treated controls. No significant body-weight loss or overt signs of distress were observed under the experimental conditions.ConclusionHAdV-3-TZ01 retains the characteristic human epithelial tropism of HAdV-3 and exhibits efficient viral genome amplification in human epithelial-derived cells, apoptosis induction, and measurable antitumor activity in vivo. The apoptosis difference between HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 should be interpreted cautiously because the analysis was limited to 293F cells and did not establish a tumor-specific pro-apoptotic mechanism. As an unmodified respiratory pathogen, HAdV-3-TZ01 should not be considered a directly translatable therapeutic agent. Rather, these findings support HAdV-3-TZ01 as a potential starting backbone for future genetic engineering aimed at improving tumor selectivity and safety. 2Materials and methods2.1Cells and virusesHEK293FT, A549, BEAS-2B, H3122, MRC-5, and L929 cell lines were maintained in our laboratory. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (#BC-M-005, BioChannel, China) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (#BC-SE-FBS07, BioChannel, China) at 37 °C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO2. HEK293FT cells (an adherent derivative of HEK293 expressing the SV40 large T antigen) were used for virus propagation and TCID50 titration. 293F cells (a suspension-adapted derivative of HEK293 maintained in serum-free medium) were used exclusively for apoptosis analysis. Both cell lines are derived from human embryonic kidney cells and are not tumor-derived. The suspension growth characteristics of 293F cells facilitate uniform cell preparation and flow cytometric analysis. HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 used in the comparative apoptosis assay were propagated and titrated using the same HEK293FT cell system to ensure consistency of viral preparations. Wild-type human adenovirus type 5 (HAdV-5) was obtained from Guangzhou Paizhen Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (#WRS-240802, Guangzhou, China). The HAdV-3 isolate used in this study, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, was isolated from a clinical throat swab specimen and propagated in HEK293FT cells before characterization and subsequent experiments.2.2Clinical sample collection and virus isolationA throat swab specimen was collected from a 5-year-old female patient admitted to The Affiliated Taizhou People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, Taizhou, China, on May 23, 2024. The patient presented with fever and cough for 4 days before admission. Respiratory pathogen testing revealed adenovirus DNA positivity, and chest radiography indicated bronchopneumonia. The specimen was collected during hospitalization for adenovirus isolation and further characterization. Samples were transported on ice and processed within 12 h after collection. The specimen was diluted 1:1 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), clarified by centrifugation at 1,500 × g for 10 min, and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. The filtrate was supplemented with penicillin (100 IU/mL) and streptomycin (100 μg/mL) before inoculation.HEK293FT cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. For virus isolation, confluent HEK293FT cell monolayers were inoculated with clarified clinical specimens and incubated for 2 h to allow viral adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, fresh maintenance medium containing 2% FBS was added. Cells were monitored daily for cytopathic effects (CPE). Blind passaging was performed every 5–7 days in the absence of visible CPE. Virus-containing supernatants were harvested following the appearance of characteristic adenoviral CPE, clarified by low-speed centrifugation, aliquoted, and stored at −80 °C. Third-passage (P3) virus stocks were used for subsequent experiments.For in vivo administration, the P3 virus stock was concentrated by sucrose cushion ultracentrifugation. Briefly, virus-containing supernatants together with infected cell pellets were subjected to three cycles of freeze–thaw (−80 °C/37 °C) to release intracellular viral particles, followed by low-speed centrifugation (3,000 × g, 4 °C, 20 min) to remove cellular debris. The clarified supernatant was layered onto a 20% sucrose cushion prepared in PBS (pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 100,000 × g for 2 h at 4 °C. The viral pellet was resuspended in sterile PBS and stored at −80 °C. The resulting concentrated virus stock was used for subsequent in vivo experiments. The viral titer was determined by TCID50 assay as described below, yielding 3.16 × 1011 TCID50/mL.2.3Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysisTransmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis was performed by Shanghai Weishi Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Briefly, 5 μL of virus-enriched sample was placed onto a Formvar–carbon-coated copper grid and incubated for 5 min, followed by blotting with filter paper. The samples were fixed with 1% glutaraldehyde (final concentration) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) for 1 min. After washing with phosphate buffer, the grids were negatively stained with 1% uranyl acetate. Images were acquired using a transmission electron microscope (Talos 120, FEI, USA) according to standard operating procedures.2.4Virus titration by TCID50 assayVirus infectivity was determined by a tissue culture infectious dose 50% (TCID50) assay in 293FT cells. Briefly, 293FT cells were seeded into 96-well plates at 1 × 104 cells per well and cultured overnight. Virus stocks were serially diluted 10-fold in DMEM containing 2% FBS, and 100 μL of each dilution was added to eight replicate wells. After incubation at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere, the wells were monitored daily for the appearance of cytopathic effects (CPE). CPE-positive and CPE-negative wells were recorded at 3 days post-infection, and viral titers were calculated using the Reed–Muench method and expressed as TCID50/mL.2.5Viral identification and whole-genome sequencingViral DNA was extracted from infected-cell culture supernatants using a Universal Genomic DNA Kit (#CW2298M, Cowin Biotech Co., Ltd., China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Preliminary species identification was performed using a previously described multiplex PCR assay targeting conserved regions of the adenoviral hexon gene (Xu et al., 2000). PCR products were purified and subjected to Sanger sequencing. Consensus sequences were compared against the NCBI nucleotide database using BLAST for preliminary virus typing.For whole-genome characterization, viral genomic DNA was submitted to a commercial sequencing service provider for next-generation sequencing. Sequencing libraries were prepared according to standard protocols and sequenced using paired-end 150-bp reads on an Illumina NovaSeq platform. Raw sequencing reads were subjected to quality control and de novo assembly to obtain the complete viral genome sequence. Open reading frames were annotated based on sequence homology with representative adenovirus reference genomes available in GenBank.2.6Phylogenetic and recombination analysesRepresentative human adenovirus reference sequences were retrieved from GenBank. Multiple sequence alignments were generated using MEGA version 11 (Tamura et al., 2021). The optimal nucleotide substitution model was selected using the “Find Best DNA/Protein Models” function implemented in MEGA. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using the maximum-likelihood method with 1,000 bootstrap replicates.Potential recombination events were identified using RDP4 (v4.101) with multiple detection algorithms under default settings (Martin et al., 2015). Putative recombination signals were further evaluated using SimPlot (v3.5.1) based on similarity plot and bootscanning analyses (Lole et al., 1999).2.7Comparative apoptosis analysis293F cells (a suspension-adapted derivative of HEK293 maintained in serum-free medium) were used for this assay. This cell line was chosen because its suspension growth characteristics facilitate uniform cell preparation and high-throughput flow cytometric analysis, which is technically advantageous for detecting subtle differences in apoptotic populations. Cells were cultured in Trans CD05 medium (#YYCD05, Youyi Biotechnology, China) at 37 °C with 5% CO2 in a shaking incubator (125 rpm). Cells were infected with HAdV-3 or HAdV-5 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.001. HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 used in this comparative assay were propagated and titrated using the same HEK293FT cell system to ensure consistency of viral preparations. Following infection, cell samples were collected at 48 h post-infection for apoptosis analysis.Apoptosis was assessed using an Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (#C1062M, Beyotime, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed once with cold PBS, and resuspended in Annexin V binding buffer. Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI) were added sequentially, and samples were incubated for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. Flow cytometric analysis was performed using a CaleCyter2080 flow cytometer (Calerio, China). At least 10,000 events were acquired for each sample.Data were analyzed using FlowJo V10 software. Viable cells, early apoptotic cells (Annexin V+/PI−), and late apoptotic cells (Annexin V+/PI+) were quantified. Total apoptosis was defined as the sum of early and late apoptotic populations. All experiments were performed in three independent biological replicates.2.8Cell tropism and viral genome amplificationHuman lung carcinoma A549 cells, human bronchial epithelial BEAS-2B cells, human lung adenocarcinoma H3122 cells, human lung fibroblast MRC-5 cells, human embryonic kidney 293FT cells, and murine fibroblast L929 cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS.Cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells per well and infected with HAdV-3-TZ01 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1, calculated based on TCID50 titers. Following viral adsorption for 1–2 h, the inoculum was removed and replaced with fresh maintenance medium. Mock-infected cells received culture medium alone. Samples were collected at 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-infection for viral genome quantification. Total cellular DNA was extracted using a Universal Genomic DNA Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Viral genome levels were quantified by quantitative PCR (qPCR) targeting the conserved adenoviral hexon gene region using previously described primers (Qiu et al., 2018). Primer sequences are listed in Table 1. The β-actin gene was used as an internal reference for normalization.Table 1Primers used for quantitative PCR analysis.Target genePrimerSequence (5′–3′)Amplicon size (bp)ReferenceAdenovirus hexonHexon-FAGACATGACHTTYGAGGTGGAYCC122 Qiu et al. (2018) Adenovirus hexonHexon-RCGCAGGTASACBGYYTCRA122 Qiu et al. (2018) β-actinActin-FGAGGCCCAGAGCAAGAGAG107This studyβ-actinActin-RTTGTAGAAGGTGTGGTGCCAG107This studyPrimer sequences used for quantification of adenoviral genome copy numbers by qPCR. The adenoviral hexon gene was used for viral genome detection, and β-actin served as the internal reference gene. Amplicon sizes and literature sources are indicated.qPCR reactions were performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (#11184ES08, Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) on a Gentier 96R Real-Time PCR System (Xi’an Tianlong Science and Technology Co., Ltd.) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Relative viral genome levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method. Viral genome levels at different time points were normalized to the 12 hpi sample within each cell line, which was defined as the baseline level, and normalized values were transformed to log10 scale for visualization and statistical analysis. Three independent biological replicates were performed for each condition.Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism. Differences among cell types and infection time points were analyzed using two-way ANOVA with interaction effects, followed by Šídák’s multiple comparisons test. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.2.9Xenograft tumor model and in vivo evaluationSixteen female BALB/c-nu nude mice (4 weeks old, weighing approximately 18–20 g) were used in this study. Sample size (n = 8 per group) was determined empirically based on previous experience with this tumor model. Each mouse was subcutaneously inoculated in the right axillary region with 4 × 106 A549-luciferase (A549-Luc) cells suspended in 100 μL PBS. Tumor growth was monitored every 3 days using digital calipers, and tumor volume was calculated using the formula V = L × W2/2, where L represents the longest diameter and W represents the shortest diameter.When tumors reached approximately 100 mm3, mice were stratified according to tumor volume and randomly assigned to treatment and control groups (n = 8 per group) using a computer-generated randomization sequence. Mice in the treatment group received intratumoral injections of HAdV-3-TZ01 (50 μL per dose, containing 1.58 × 1010 TCID50; stock titer: 3.16 × 1011 TCID50/mL) on days 21 and 34 after tumor implantation. The two-injection schedule (days 21 and 34, with a 13-day interval) was selected based on previously reported intratumoral dosing strategies for oncolytic adenovirus therapies. Similar dosing intervals have been evaluated in clinical studies, such as the phase 1 BETA prime trial of AdAPT-001, in which intratumoral administration of the oncolytic adenovirus was performed once every 2 weeks at the recommended phase 2 dose (Conley et al., 2024). This is consistent with the principle that sustained, multi-dose regimens can achieve superior therapeutic outcomes compared with single or short-term dosing schedules. Control mice received equal volumes of PBS following the same schedule. Tumor volume measurements and bioluminescence imaging analyses were performed by investigators blinded to group allocation.The viral dose was selected based on previously reported intratumoral administration regimens of oncolytic adenoviruses in murine xenograft models, taking into consideration the tumor size and feasibility of intratumoral administration. Preliminary tolerability observations showed no apparent body weight loss or treatment-related distress during the treatment period. Body weight was recorded throughout the study to evaluate treatment-associated toxicity. No formal dose-escalation or dose-optimization study was performed.Mice were monitored daily for signs of distress or discomfort throughout the study. Humane endpoints were defined as tumor volume exceeding 1,500 mm3, tumor ulceration, >20% body weight loss, or signs of severe pain/distress. Animals reaching humane endpoints were euthanized by CO2 inhalation followed by cervical dislocation. No animals were excluded from the analysis.All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (Approval No. 2410053).2.10Bioluminescence imagingTumor burden was monitored by bioluminescence imaging (BLI) on days 20, 22, 32, and 43 after tumor implantation. Mice received intraperitoneal injections of D-luciferin (#40901ES01, Yeasen, China) (15 mg/mL) at 10 μL/g body weight approximately 15 min before imaging. The patient presented with fever and cough for 4 days before admission. Respiratory pathogen testing revealed adenovirus DNA positivity, and chest radiography indicated bronchopneumonia. The specimen was collected during hospitalization for adenovirus isolation and further characterization. Samples were transported on ice and processed within 12 h after collection. The specimen was diluted 1:1 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), clarified by centrifugation at 1,500 × g for 10 min, and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. The filtrate was supplemented with penicillin (100 IU/mL) and streptomycin (100 μg/mL) before inoculation.HEK293FT cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. For virus isolation, confluent HEK293FT cell monolayers were inoculated with clarified clinical specimens and incubated for 2 h to allow viral adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, fresh maintenance medium containing 2% FBS was added. Cells were monitored daily for cytopathic effects (CPE). Blind passaging was performed every 5–7 days in the absence of visible CPE. Virus-containing supernatants were harvested following the appearance of characteristic adenoviral CPE, clarified by low-speed centrifugation, aliquoted, and stored at −80 °C. Third-passage (P3) virus stocks were used for subsequent experiments.For in vivo administration, the P3 virus stock was concentrated by sucrose cushion ultracentrifugation. full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Isolation and genomic characterization of HAdV-3-TZ01A clinical adenovirus isolate, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, was recovered from a throat swab sample collected from a patient presenting with mild respiratory symptoms. (A) Representative micrograph of HEK293FT cells showing typical cytopathic effects induced by HAdV-3-TZ01 during virus isolation and propagation. Representative images obtained during the third passage. Scale bar = 100 μm; magnification 100×; imaging conditions (bright-field microscopy). (B) Representative micrograph of mock-treated HEK293FT cells showing normal cell morphology. Scale bar = 100 μm; magnification 100×; imaging conditions (bright-field microscopy). (C) Agarose gel electrophoresis analysis of multiplex PCR products used for adenovirus typing. Viral supernatants collected from infected HEK293FT cells were used as templates for multiplex PCR amplification with previously reported primer sets. PCR products were separated on a 1% agarose gel and visualized using a gel imaging system. Lane M indicates the DNA molecular weight marker. (D) Representative transmission electron micrograph of HAdV-3-TZ01 particles concentrated by low-speed centrifugation (13,000 rpm). Adenovirus-like particles with characteristic morphology were observed (scale bar = 100 nm).Panel A shows a light microscopy image of sparse, scattered adherent cells with irregular shapes and extensions, scale bar indicating one hundred micrometers. Panel B displays a denser layer of adherent cells with similar morphology, also at one hundred micrometers scale. Panel C presents an agarose gel electrophoresis result with clearly defined DNA bands for samples labeled M, A-D,F, B,D,E, B,C,E, and B,C,D, with bands near one thousand base pairs. Panel D is a grayscale transmission electron micrograph showing a single, spherical particle, likely a virus, centered on a plain background with a scale bar of one hundred nanometers.To determine the identity of the isolate, viral DNA was extracted from infected-cell supernatants and subjected to multiplex PCR using previously described adenovirus species-specific primer sets targeting conserved regions of the hexon gene. As shown in Figure 1C, amplification products of approximately 750–1,000 bp were detected with multiple primer combinations. The observed amplification profile was consistent with species B adenoviruses and differed from the characteristic patterns reported for other adenovirus species. Subsequent Sanger sequencing of the PCR products confirmed that the isolate belonged to human adenovirus species B and shared the highest sequence similarity with human adenovirus type 3 (HAdV-3).Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) further revealed viral particles with typical adenoviral morphology (Figure 1D), providing additional structural confirmation of the isolate.To further characterize the isolate, whole-genome sequencing was performed using high-throughput sequencing technology (Figure 2A). The complete viral genome was assembled and compared with representative human adenovirus reference strains. Phylogenetic analysis based on the full-length genome demonstrated that the isolate clustered robustly with HAdV-3 strains and was clearly separated from other adenovirus types (Figure 2B). Consistent results were obtained using analyses of major capsid genes, confirming the classification of the isolate as HAdV-3 (Figures 2C–E). (A) Schematic representation of the complete genome organization of HAdV-3-TZ01. Major early (E1A, E1B, E2, E3, and E4), intermediate (IX and IVa2), and late (L1–L5) transcription units, as well as the inverted terminal repeats (ITRs), are indicated according to their genomic locations and transcriptional orientations. Representative genes, including hexon, penton base, fiber, DNA polymerase, pre-terminal protein (pTP), DNA-binding protein (DBP), and 100 K, are labeled. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn the present study, we isolated and characterized a contemporary clinical HAdV-3 strain, HAdV-3-TZ01. Genomic analysis confirmed that HAdV-3-TZ01 belonged to HAdV-3 and retained the characteristic genetic features of currently circulating strains. Functional characterization revealed robust viral genome replication in human respiratory epithelial cells and multiple epithelial-derived tumor cell lines. Intratumoral administration significantly inhibited tumor growth in an A549 xenograft model, with no detectable body weight loss or overt signs of distress under the experimental conditions. These findings provide updated biological insights into a naturally circulating HAdV-3 isolate and suggest its potential value as an alternative adenoviral backbone for oncolytic virotherapy.The viral genome replication characteristics of HAdV-3-TZ01 were consistent with the known epithelial tropism of species B adenoviruses. Viral genome levels increased rapidly in H3122, BEAS-2B, and A549 cells, whereas replication was substantially restricted in murine L929 cells, consistent with the species specificity of human adenoviruses. Importantly, HAdV-3-TZ01 also showed active viral genome replication in several human tumor cell lines under low multiplicity conditions, suggesting that malignant epithelial cells provide a suitable environment for viral amplification. However, we did not assess receptor expression levels (CD46, DSG2, or CAR) in the cell lines tested, nor did we directly compare viral replication or cytotoxicity between malignant and non-malignant human cells. Such comparisons will be important for evaluating tumor selectivity in future studies.HAdV-3-TZ01 infection induced apoptotic cell death in infected cells. However, the apoptosis analysis in the present study was performed exclusively in 293F cells (a non-tumorigenic HEK293-derived cell line), and the absolute increase in total apoptotic cells relative to mock infection was modest (approximately 4.5 percentage points). Moreover, equal TCID50-based MOIs do not guarantee equivalent viral entry efficiency due to distinct receptor usage, and we did not assess early infection kinetics or apoptosis-associated molecular markers. Whether HAdV-3-TZ01 induces enhanced apoptosis in tumor-relevant cell lines such as A549 or H3122, or exhibits differential cytotoxicity compared with non-malignant epithelial cells such as BEAS-2B, remains to be determined. Previous studies have demonstrated that HAdV-3 infection can activate an intrinsic apoptosis-associated cell death program in A549 cells, accompanied by the release of extracellular vesicles containing cellular stress and apoptotic markers. These findings provide mechanistic support for further investigation of apoptosis-related pathways induced by HAdV-3-TZ01, particularly in tumor-relevant cellular contexts. Most clinically evaluated oncolytic adenoviruses have been developed based on engineered HAdV-5 platforms. Species B adenoviruses, including HAdV-3, utilize distinct cellular receptors from HAdV-5 and may therefore exhibit different patterns of cellular tropism. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of HAdV-3 as an oncolytic platform; for example, the engineered HAdV-3-based vector Ad3-hTERT-E1A showed selective replication and antitumor activity across multiple cancer types while maintaining reduced toxicity in non-malignant cells (Hemminki et al., 2011). However, these studies primarily focused on genetically modified viral vectors optimized for therapeutic applications. In contrast, HAdV-3-TZ01 represents a naturally occurring clinical isolate that showed antitumor activity in vitro and in vivo without prior genetic modification. Therefore, the novelty of this study does not lie in demonstrating that HAdV-3 can infect tumor cells, but rather in providing a comprehensive characterization of a contemporary circulating HAdV-3 isolate by integrating genomic features, comparative replication properties, and preliminary in vivo antitumor activity. HAdV-3-TZ01 is a wild-type respiratory pathogen that retains efficient viral genome amplification in non-malignant bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B); therefore, rather than serving as an immediate therapeutic agent, this isolate provides a valuable starting platform for future genetic engineering aimed at achieving tumor selectivity and attenuated pathogenicity. Genomic analysis identified a short HAdV-7-derived recombinant fragment within the HAdV-3-TZ01 genome. Despite this recombinant region, the overall genomic architecture and major structural proteins remained highly conserved. Whether this fragment contributes to the biological characteristics of HAdV-3-TZ01 requires further investigation.The antitumor effect observed in the A549 xenograft model—approximately 54% reduction in tumor volume and ~50% reduction in bioluminescence signal at day 43—provides consistent evidence of antitumor activity following intratumoral administration. The A549 xenograft model has been widely used for evaluating the in vivo efficacy of oncolytic adenoviruses, including conditionally replicative adenovirus platforms, allowing comparison with previous reports. For instance, studies on the well-known oncolytic adenovirus ONYX-015 have employed this model to demonstrate its antitumor efficacy following systemic or intratumoral administration (Heise et al., 1999). More recently, the A549 xenograft model has also been used to evaluate armed conditionally replicating adenoviruses, such as a p14 FAST protein-expressing vector, which induced widespread syncytium formation and reduced tumor growth rates in vivo (Del Papa et al., 2019). Although H3122 cells showed the highest viral genome accumulation in vitro, A549-Luc cells were selected for the in vivo studies because they provide consistent tumor establishment, reproducible growth kinetics, and reliable longitudinal bioluminescence monitoring. Nevertheless, direct evidence linking the observed tumor inhibition to sustained viral replication and intratumoral spread remains unavailable. Specifically, we did not evaluate longitudinal viral genome kinetics or recover infectious progeny viruses from tumor tissues, nor did we perform spatial analyses of viral distribution through adenoviral antigen staining or functional assessment of tumor cell death by histological markers. These limitations do not negate the observed antitumor efficacy but highlight the need for future studies integrating virological and pathological analyses to define the mechanisms underlying HAdV-3-TZ01-mediated tumor suppression. The dosing schedule employed in this study (two intratumoral injections on days 21 and 34, with a 13-day interval) is supported by precedents in the field, where repeated intratumoral administrations at approximately 2-week intervals have been evaluated in both preclinical and clinical settings. For instance, in the phase 1 BETA prime trial, the oncolytic adenovirus AdAPT-001 was administered intratumorally once every 2 weeks at the recommended phase 2 dose (Conley et al., 2024). Furthermore, studies have suggested that increasing the number of injections, rather than the dose per injection, may be a more effective strategy to enhance therapeutic outcomes.Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. First, viral replication was evaluated primarily through intracellular viral DNA quantification, which does not directly measure infectious progeny production. Second, the apoptosis analysis was limited to 293F cells and did not include tumor-relevant or non-malignant epithelial controls. Third, receptor expression levels were not examined, and early entry efficiency was not assessed. Fourth, in vivo evaluation was limited to a single xenograft model with intratumoral administration, constraining generalizability rather than undermining the A549 results. full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionHuman adenovirus type 3 (HAdV-3) is a major cause of adenovirus-associated respiratory disease in China and is frequently associated with outbreaks among children and young adults (Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). In China, HAdV-3 has consistently been identified as a major contributor to adenovirus-associated respiratory diseases and is often linked to severe pneumonia and community-wide epidemics (Chen et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2024). Despite extensive epidemiological surveillance, the biological characteristics of newly circulating HAdV-3 strains remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to their replication properties and potential biomedical applications.Beyond their role as important respiratory pathogens, adenoviruses have attracted considerable attention as versatile platforms for gene delivery, vaccine development, and cancer therapy (Sato-Dahlman et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023). Their well-characterized genome, high transduction efficiency, large transgene carrying capacity, and established manufacturing processes have facilitated the development of numerous adenovirus-based therapeutics. In recent years, oncolytic adenoviruses have emerged as a promising class of anticancer agents capable of selectively replicating within tumor cells and inducing direct tumor lysis while simultaneously stimulating antitumor immune responses (Tazawa et al., 2017; van Beusechem et al., 2002). Several adenovirus-based oncolytic therapeutics have advanced into clinical development. For example, CG0070 (cretostimogene grenadenorepvec), an oncolytic adenovirus expressing GM-CSF, has demonstrated clinical activity in patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (Tang et al., 2026). In addition, various engineered adenoviral platforms expressing immunomodulatory transgenes are currently being investigated in preclinical and clinical studies (Grandi et al., 2023; Watanabe et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022).Historically, HAdV-5 has been the predominant backbone for the development of oncolytic adenoviruses (Gao et al., 2020; Qian et al., 2025). Although HAdV-5-based vectors have demonstrated promising therapeutic potential, their high seroprevalence of neutralizing antibodies and dependence on specific cellular receptors may limit their performance in certain clinical settings (Hong et al., 2025). For example, while HAdV-5 neutralizing antibodies are highly prevalent in the population, the seroprevalence of HAdV-3 neutralizing antibodies in children is relatively low (12.07–33.96%), suggesting that HAdV-3-based vectors may potentially encounter fewer pre-existing immunity constraints (Lu et al., 2023). In addition, species B adenoviruses such as HAdV-3 utilize alternative cellular receptors, including CD46 and desmoglein-2 (DSG2) (Gaggar et al., 2003; Hensen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2011), which are broadly expressed in epithelial tissues and many human malignancies (Sharma et al., 2009). Nevertheless, the biological properties and therapeutic potential of naturally circulating HAdV-3 isolates remain insufficiently characterized.In the present study, we isolated a contemporary clinical HAdV-3 strain, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, from a patient with acute respiratory infection. Using whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis, we characterized its genetic features and evaluated its viral genome amplification capacity in respiratory epithelial and tumor-derived cell lines. In addition, we compared the apoptotic responses between HAdV-3-TZ01 and HAdV-5 during infection spread and assessed its antitumor efficacy in an A549-luciferase xenograft mouse model. papers.title_original: Biological characterization of a clinical human adenovirus type 3 isolate with oncolytic potential

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to characterize a contemporary clinical HAdV-3 isolate and evaluate its viral genome amplification, apoptosis induction, and antitumor activity. The biological characteristics of newly circulating HAdV-3 strains remain incompletely understood, particularly with respect to their replication properties and potential biomedical applications.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A clinical HAdV-3 isolate, designated HAdV-3-TZ01, was recovered from a throat swab specimen from a patient with adenovirus-associated respiratory disease. The study evaluated viral genome amplification in human respiratory-related and tumor-derived cell lines and a murine cell line. Antitumor activity was assessed in an A549-luciferase xenograft model in BALB/c-nu nude mice.
analysis.methods: Viral identity and genomic characteristics were determined using multiplex PCR, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and recombination analysis. Viral genome amplification kinetics were evaluated in human respiratory-related and tumor-derived cell lines and a murine cell line by quantitative PCR. HEK293FT cells were used for virus propagation and TCID50 titration, while 293F cells were used exclusively for apoptosis analysis.
analysis.main_results: Genomic and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that HAdV-3-TZ01 belonged to HAdV-3 within species B and exhibited a genomic backbone highly conserved with contemporary circulating HAdV-3 strains. Functional characterization revealed robust viral genome replication in human respiratory epithelial cells and multiple epithelial-derived tumor cell lines. Viral genome levels increased rapidly in H3122, BEAS-2B, and A549 cells, whereas replication was substantially restricted in murine L929 cells. HAdV-3-TZ01 also showed active viral genome replication in several human tumor cell lines under low multiplicity conditions.

papers.title: Assessment of the Necessity for High-Level Disinfection (HLD) of Reusable Ophthalmic Devices: A Multisociety Position Paper.
papers.abstract: Regulatory agencies in the United States and abroad are increasingly citing clinics and surgical facilities for what they deem to be inadequate disinfection of Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) tips, gonioscopy lenses, laser lenses, and other reusable clinic devices that contact the ocular surface. These regulators require routine high-level disinfection (HLD) of these reusable devices to prevent infection transmission. A multisociety task force formed to assess the necessity of HLD found no published evidence that these devices transmit sight-threatening infections or that HLD reduces infection transmission compared with lower-level disinfection methods. Meanwhile, routine use of chemical HLD reduces clinic efficiency, increases healthcare costs and waste, and may damage device surfaces potentially affecting patient care. Underlying these mandates for HLD is the nearly century-old Spaulding classification system, which inappropriately groups the ocular surface with heavily contaminated mucous membranes. A task force survey with more than 1000 ophthalmologist respondents found that the most common reprocessing methods were alcohol wiping for GAT tips and either alcohol wiping or soap and water for diagnostic or laser lenses. Many respondents using chemical HLD reported adverse effects, including ocular surface chemical toxicity and device damage. Despite infrequent use of HLD, reported infection transmission was exceedingly rare and generally limited to self-limited adenoviral conjunctivitis. The task force agreed with the majority (88%) of ophthalmologists surveyed that HLD should not be required for these reusable devices in routine clinical care. Instead, HLD should be a discretionary consideration in higher-risk circumstances, such as following use of these devices in patients with suspected infection. This paper presents the summary recommendations of a policy statement approved by the American Academy of Ophthalmology Board of Trustees and endorsed by four subspecialty societies.

These regulators require routine high-level disinfection (HLD) of these reusable devices to prevent infection transmission. A multisociety task force formed to assess the necessity of HLD found no published evidence that these devices transmit sight-threatening infections or that HLD reduces infection transmission compared with lower-level disinfection methods. Meanwhile, routine use of chemical HLD reduces clinic efficiency, increases healthcare costs and waste, and may damage device surfaces potentially affecting patient care. Underlying these mandates for HLD is the nearly century-old Spaulding classification system, which inappropriately groups the ocular surface with heavily contaminated mucous membranes. A task force survey with more than 1000 ophthalmologist respondents found that the most common reprocessing methods were alcohol wiping for GAT tips and either alcohol wiping or soap and water for diagnostic or laser lenses. Many respondents using chemical HLD reported adverse effects, including ocular surface chemical toxicity and device damage. Despite infrequent use of HLD, reported infection transmission was exceedingly rare and generally limited to self-limited adenoviral conjunctivitis. The task force agreed with the majority (88%) of ophthalmologists surveyed that HLD should not be required for these reusable devices in routine clinical care. Instead, HLD should be a discretionary consideration in higher-risk circumstances, such as following use of these devices in patients with suspected infection. This paper presents the summary recommendations of a policy statement approved by the American Academy of Ophthalmology Board of Trustees and endorsed by four subspecialty societies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Regulatory agencies are increasingly citing clinics for inadequate disinfection of reusable ophthalmic devices, raising concerns about the necessity of high-level disinfection (HLD) for preventing infection transmission. The study aimed to evaluate whether HLD is required for these devices.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A multisociety task force was formed to assess the necessity of HLD for reusable ophthalmic devices. The study involved more than 1000 ophthalmologist respondents across various clinics and surgical facilities.
analysis.methods: The task force conducted a survey to gather data on current reprocessing methods, reported adverse effects, and infection transmission rates associated with the use of these devices. They also reviewed the scientific basis of HLD requirements and compared them with alternative disinfection methods.
analysis.main_results: No published evidence was found that these devices transmit sight-threatening infections or that HLD reduces infection transmission compared with lower-level disinfection methods. Many respondents using chemical HLD reported adverse effects, including ocular surface chemical toxicity and device damage.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the mandates for HLD are based on outdated classification systems and that the practice may not be necessary for routine clinical care. This is a novel conclusion based on the task force's findings and survey data.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that HLD may not be required for routine clinical use of these devices, which could reduce healthcare costs and improve clinic efficiency. This has implications for infection control practices and the management of reusable ophthalmic equipment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on survey data and does not include direct experimental evidence on infection transmission. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on expert opinion and reported outcomes rather than rigorous clinical trials.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the necessity of high-level disinfection (HLD) for reusable ophthalmic devices, such as Goldmann applanation tonometry tips and gonioscopy lenses. It highlights that regulatory mandates for HLD are based on outdated systems and that no published evidence supports its requirement for preventing sight-threatening infections. Instead, the authors suggest that HLD should be a discretionary measure in higher-risk situations. The findings imply that HLD may not be essential for routine clinical care, potentially reducing costs and improving efficiency. However, the study's reliance on survey data limits its evidence strength, and further research is needed to confirm these conclusions.

papers.full_text: IntroductionHeat- and moisture-sensitive porous materials such as plush toys, paper products, and foam are widely used in pediatric and healthcare environments but cannot be decontaminated by conventional liquid disinfectants, heat, or UV-based methods. This creates a need for alternative dry, non-thermal technologies. Non-thermal plasma (NTP) offers a promising approach for disinfecting such materials without compromising their integrity.MethodsIn this study, we assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber.ResultsMaterial characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Across all substrates, NTP treatment produced time-dependent reductions in viral infectivity. Maximum reductions ranged from 5.5–6.3 log10 for SARS-CoV-2, 6.3–7.1 log10 for IAV, 4.0–5.9 log10 for HAdV, and 2.7–5.0 log10 for HRV, depending on the virus-material combination. Enveloped viruses (SARS-CoV-2 and IAV) were inactivated more rapidly than the non-enveloped viruses HAdV and HRV, although all viruses were reduced to nearly or completely undetectable levels after 30–60 min of treatment. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic inactivation kinetics characterized by an initial rapid decline followed by a slower phase of inactivation.DiscussionThese findings support that NTP could be an effective, residue-free, and material-preserving method for inactivating a broad spectrum of respiratory viruses on porous substrates incompatible with conventional disinfection. NTP thus might represent a valuable tool for safely reusing sensitive items in pediatric and clinical settings and reducing contamination risks where existing methods are impractical. 2Materials and methods2.1Non-thermal plasma (NTP) deviceNTP was generated by point-to-ring corona discharge in a device whose operating parameters (discharge power: 0.7 W, voltage: 6–8 kV, current: 100–150 μA) were specifically optimized for enhanced antimicrobial and virucidal efficacy. The optimization process is described in detail in our previous works (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Klenivskyi et al., 2024), which involved systematic variation of the interelectrode distance (0–8 mm) and discharge current (50–500 μA) and assessment of the bactericidal effect on Escherichia coli. The selected parameters represent the optimal balance between maximum antimicrobial activity and stable, spark-free discharge operation.Further details of the NTP device and the concentrations of long-lived plasma-generated species (NO2, N2O, O3, and H2O2) measured under identical operating conditions were described in our previous study (Bouazizi et al., 2024).2.2Assessment of material damage by NTP using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)Material morphology and surface structure were examined by SEM using a Vega II LSH instrument (TESCAN GROUP, a.s., Brno, Czech Republic) to visualize potential NTP-induced alterations accurately. Small pieces were cut from the samples and mounted on a sample holder using double-sided conductive adhesive tape. All specimens were then sputter-coated with a thin gold layer under an argon atmosphere (15 mA, 60 s) using a POLARON Emitech SC7640 sputter coater (Quorum Technologies Ltd., Lewes, UK). Imaging parameters, including accelerating voltage (kV), working distance (WD; mm), and magnification, are provided at the bottom of the corresponding images in the Results section.2.3Chemical composition analysis of material surface using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed to characterize the chemical composition of the sample surfaces to a depth of ~5 nm using an Axis Ultra DLD spectrometer (Kratos Analytical Ltd., UK). A monochromatic Al Kα (hν = 1486.7 eV) X-ray source operating at 75 W (5 mA, 15 kV) was used, and spectra were collected over a 300 × 700 μm analytical area. High-resolution spectra were acquired with a step size of 0.1 eV and a pass energy of 20 eV. The Kratos charge neutralizer system was used for all analyses. The instrument base pressure during measurements was consistently 2 × 10−8 Pa. Spectra were analyzed using CasaXPS software (version 2.3.17) and charge-corrected to the main C 1 s carbon component (C–C, C–H), set to 285.00 eV. A set of control samples was placed in another device that did not produce NTP. Subsequently, the inoculum was overlaid with 3% carboxymethyl cellulose in DMEM/PenStrep/10% FBS and incubated for 5 days at 37 °C and 5% CO2. full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionHeat- and moisture-sensitive porous materials such as plush toys, paper products, and foam are widely used in pediatric and healthcare environments but cannot be decontaminated by conventional liquid disinfectants, heat, or UV-based methods. This creates a need for alternative dry, non-thermal technologies. Non-thermal plasma (NTP) offers a promising approach for disinfecting such materials without compromising their integrity.MethodsIn this study, we assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber.ResultsMaterial characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Across all substrates, NTP treatment produced time-dependent reductions in viral infectivity. Maximum reductions ranged from 5.5–6.3 log10 for SARS-CoV-2, 6.3–7.1 log10 for IAV, 4.0–5.9 log10 for HAdV, and 2.7–5.0 log10 for HRV, depending on the virus-material combination. Enveloped viruses (SARS-CoV-2 and IAV) were inactivated more rapidly than the non-enveloped viruses HAdV and HRV, although all viruses were reduced to nearly or completely undetectable levels after 30–60 min of treatment. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic inactivation kinetics characterized by an initial rapid decline followed by a slower phase of inactivation.DiscussionThese findings support that NTP could be an effective, residue-free, and material-preserving method for inactivating a broad spectrum of respiratory viruses on porous substrates incompatible with conventional disinfection. NTP thus might represent a valuable tool for safely reusing sensitive items in pediatric and clinical settings and reducing contamination risks where existing methods are impractical.

full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Non-thermal plasma has limited impact on sensitive materialsTo assess the impact of NTP on the structural integrity of sensitive materials, SEM imaging was performed on untreated and NTP-treated samples. Microscopic examination of untreated and NTP-treated samples revealed distinct material-specific behaviors. The paper substrate showed no substantial morphological alterations following NTP exposure when comparing the reference sample (Figure 1A) with the sample after 24 h of NTP treatment (Figure 1B). Plush fabric fibers maintained a smooth surface devoid of defects, fractures, or adherent particles. However, a slight increase in fiber coiling and twisting was observed, which may be related to the localized effects of NTP on surface tension or structural elasticity (Figures 1C,D). In contrast, the foam rubber sample exhibited inherently high porosity, with numerous micrometer-scale particles uniformly distributed across its surface (Figure 1F). NTP treatment did not induce discernible changes in the morphology or abundance of these particles, suggesting limited susceptibility to surface modifications under the applied NTP conditions (Figure 1E). In summary, paper showed no detectable structural changes, plush fabric exhibited only minor alterations, and foam rubber maintained its structural integrity after treatment.Figure 1SEM images of untreated and NTP-treated materials (A) NTP-untreated paper at 2500 × magnification; (B) paper after 24 h of NTP at 2500 × magnification; (C) NTP-untreated plush fabric at 1000 × magnification; (D) plush fabric after 24 h of NTP exposure at 1000 × magnification; (E) NTP-untreated foam rubber at 1500 × magnification; (F) foam rubber after 24 h of NTP exposure at 1500 × magnification. SEM: scanning electron microscopy, NTP: non-thermal plasma.Panel A shows a scanning electron microscope image of dense, overlapping fibrous structures with rough surfaces. Panel B features similarly intertwined fibers but with distinct spacing and visible gaps. Panel C displays thin, elongated fibers arranged in a more open, upright orientation. Panel D highlights comparable thin fibers, some crossing and extending at various angles. Panel E presents a porous network with irregularly shaped holes and interconnected fibrous edges. Panel F depicts a similar porous structure with fibrous walls and cavity-like spaces. All panels demonstrate varying microstructures of fibrous or porous material under high magnification.3.2Superficial oxidation of the material surfaces exposed to NTP analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)3.2.1PaperXPS analysis was performed to quantify the surface chemical modifications induced by plasma treatment. The elemental composition of the untreated reference sample was 58.7 at.% carbon and 41.3 at.% oxygen. Following 24 h of NTP exposure, a clear shift in surface chemistry was observed: the carbon content decreased to 55.5 at.%, while the oxygen concentration increased to 42.9 at.% (Figures 2A,B). This increase in oxygen content is consistent with the surface oxidation of cellulose occurring during air plasma discharge. Additionally, the analysis detected the incorporation of 1.6 at.% nitrogen in the samples treated for 24 h (Figure 2B).Figure 2Spectra of chemical composition analysis of paper surface, (A) unexposed to NTP, (B) after 24 h of NTP exposure. Ref: reference, NTP: non-thermal plasma.Two-panel figure showing X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results for paper samples. Panel A displays the reference paper with C 1s peak deconvolution and corresponding full survey spectrum. Panel B displays paper treated with non-thermal plasma for 24 hours, featuring C 1s and N 1s peak deconvolution and a corresponding survey, where new nitrogen-containing peaks appear. Binding energy is shown in electron volts on the x-axes.The high-resolution C 1 s spectra (Figures 2A,B) were resolved into components corresponding to C-C/C-H (284.8 eV), C-O (~286.6 eV), and O-C-O (~288.1 eV). Furthermore, a distinct signal identified at 289.7 eV was attributed to carbon atoms bonded to nitrooxy groups (-O-NO2). The formation of these organic functionalities was further supported by the high-resolution N 1 s spectra (Figure 2B), which exhibited a prominent peak at 408.0 eV, characteristic of nitrogen in a highly oxidized state within nitrooxy structures.3.2.2Plush fabricPolyester plush fabric exhibited progressive surface oxidation with increasing NTP exposure duration. The elemental composition of the untreated reference sample was 68.9 at.% carbon, 22.6 at.% oxygen, and 8.5 at.% silicon. Following 24 h of NTP exposure, the carbon content decreased to 64.0 at.%, while the oxygen concentration increased to 26.1 at.% (Figures 3A,B). Additionally, the silicon concentration rose to 9.9 at.%, likely due to plasma-induced etching of surface contaminants and subsequent exposure of the silanized layer.Figure 3Spectra of chemical composition analysis of plush fabric surface, (A) unexposed to NTP, (B) after 24 h of NTP exposure. Ref: reference, NTP: non-thermal plasma.Side-by-side comparison of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) data for “Plush - Reference” (panel A) and “Plush - 24 h NTP” (panel B), each including C 1s and Si 2p high-resolution spectra with curve fitting and assigned chemical states, and a survey scan below showing overall element signals labeled by binding energy in electron volts.High-resolution C 1 s spectra revealed that the intensity of the convoluted peak at 284.8 eV (C-C/C-H and C-Si) decreased after treatment. This change was accompanied by a marked increase in C-O bonds (~286.6 eV) and O-C=O functionalities (~288.8 eV), as well as the emergence of a new component at ~290.8 eV corresponding to carbonate species (CO32−). Alongside this extensive oxidation of the organic matrix, a substantial transformation of the silicon-based additives was also observed. The Si 2p spectra showed a significant binding-energy shift of Si 2p3/2 from ~101.8 eV (organic silicon) to ~103.3 eV, characteristic of SiO2-like structures. These findings demonstrate that NTP exposure induces a dual modification consisting of extensive oxidation of the polyester backbone and mineralization of the organosilicon surface agents.3.2.3Foam rubberAlthough the precise chemical composition of the foam rubber was unavailable, XPS analysis revealed pronounced oxidative changes following NTP treatment. The elemental composition of the untreated reference sample was 95.9 at.% carbon, 3.3 at.% oxygen, 0.6 at.% nitrogen, and a small amount of zinc (0.2 at.%), the latter likely originating from ZnO used as a vulcanization activator. Alongside these nitrogen-related modifications, broader oxidation of the polymer backbone was evident in the high-resolution C 1 s spectra. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study supports that NTP is an efficient and material-compatible method for inactivating a broad spectrum of human respiratory viruses on porous, heat- and moisture-sensitive substrates. By evaluating four epidemiologically relevant viruses—SARS-CoV-2, IAV, HAdV and HRV—across three commonly used materials in pediatric and healthcare settings (paper, plush fabric, foam rubber), we showed that NTP consistently was able to reduce viral infectivity to at least nearly undetectable levels of infectivity after 30 to 60 min, depending on virus–material combinations. These findings expand on our previous work demonstrating the virucidal effects of NTP on surface contaminants, including SARS-CoV-2 and IAV on mask filters and other materials (Obrova et al., 2022; Bouazizi et al., 2024).Material characterization provided essential insight into why all three substrates tolerated NTP exposure without major structural or chemical compromise. SEM analysis confirmed no change in structural attributes at all for paper, only minor changes for plush and foam rubber maintained its structure after treatment. XPS revealed mainly superficial oxidation—manifested as increased oxygen-containing functional groups—consistent with the mild oxidative surface modification described in prior NTP–material interaction studies (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023). Crucially, these observations were made after 24 h of continuous NTP exposure, substantially exceeding the antiviral treatment times (5–60 min), thereby providing a conservative assessment of plasma-induced surface alterations under prolonged exposure. Importantly, no detrimental alterations in material morphology were observed, supporting the suitability of NTP for items that cannot undergo heat-, moisture-, or solvent-based decontamination (Rutala et al., 2023). However, the present assessment was limited to surface morphology (SEM) and surface chemistry (XPS) and therefore could not provide a comprehensive evaluation of the mechanical performance or long-term durability of the tested materials. Regarding the durability of NTP-treated materials under realistic conditions, mechanical properties of paper exposed to NTP under comparable discharge parameters were previously evaluated and shown to remain unchanged even after 120 min of treatment (Scholtz et al., 2023). For plush fabric and foam rubber, our SEM and XPS analyses suggested that plasma treatment induces predominantly superficial surface modifications, which are unlikely to result in substantial changes in mechanical integrity. A comprehensive assessment of multi-cycle durability and mechanical properties across all tested materials is currently in progress and will be the subject of a future study.The differences in susceptibility observed among the four viruses can by some extent be explained by their structural organization and the primary molecular targets of plasma-generated RONS (Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Ahmed et al., 2025). The more pronounced initial reductions observed for SARS-CoV-2 and IAV are consistent with the high susceptibility of enveloped viruses to oxidative damage. Lipid peroxidation and modification of envelope glycoproteins can rapidly abolish infectivity even before substantial genome degradation occurs, leading to steep early declines in viable virus counts (Obrova et al., 2022; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). SARS-CoV-2 was the most susceptible virus, which is consistent with its fragile lipid envelope and the critical role of the spike glycoprotein in host-cell attachment. Oxidative damage to membrane lipids and envelope proteins can rapidly abolish infectivity even before extensive genome degradation occurs. IAV, although also enveloped, exhibited slightly greater persistence under some conditions. This may reflect differences in envelope composition, virion morphology, and the organization of its surface glycoproteins, which can influence susceptibility to oxidative modification (Obrova et al., 2022; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). In contrast, non-enveloped viruses generally depend on the accumulation of damage to capsid proteins and nucleic acids before infectivity is lost, which may result in a more gradual reduction profile (Lion, 2019; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Birmpa et al., 2016). HAdV possesses a highly stable icosahedral protein capsid composed of tightly packed structural proteins that protect the viral genome from environmental stress. Effective inactivation therefore requires the accumulation of damage to capsid proteins and/or nucleic acids, resulting in slower loss of infectivity (Lion, 2019). HRV is likewise non-enveloped and contains a compact protein capsid that contributes to its well-established environmental stability (Wang et al., 2017; Reagan et al., 1981). However, its smaller particle size and less complex capsid architecture compared with adenovirus may facilitate access of reactive species to critical viral structures, potentially explaining why HRV appeared more susceptible than HAdV despite also being non-enveloped (Huang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2017; Reagan et al., 1981). Collectively, the observed susceptibility ranking is consistent with a hierarchy in which viruses protected only by a lipid envelope are most readily inactivated, whereas viruses relying on highly stable protein capsids require more extensive molecular damage before infectivity is lost. Recent plasma-biological interface studies further indicate that plasma-generated RONS and charged particles can act synergistically on biomolecular targets by oxidizing lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids, while also inducing downstream biological responses such as oxidative stress and immune modulation, with the relative contribution of each pathway depending on virion structure (Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Ahmed et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2024).However, the dependence of inactivation kinetics seems to rely on both the material properties and virus type. Beyond the overall reduction in infectivity, the shape of the inactivation curves may provide additional insight into the underlying mechanisms of NTP-mediated viral inactivation. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic kinetics characterized by a rapid initial decrease in infectious titer followed by a slower phase of inactivation. Such tailing behavior has frequently been reported during plasma-based microbial decontamination and is generally attributed to population heterogeneity and limitations in agent accessibility rather than changes in plasma activity itself (Mošovská et al., 2023; Zhang and Wang, 2025). RONS are expected to rapidly inactivate virions that are directly exposed at the material surface, resulting in an initial steep decline. The remaining infectious fraction may consist of particles embedded within surface irregularities, retained in pores or fiber networks, or protected by aggregation and local microenvironmental effects, thereby requiring longer exposure times to achieve non-detectable levels of infectivity (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Birmpa et al., 2016; Mošovská et al., 2023; Zhang and Wang, 2025). Material-dependent differences further support the importance of physical accessibility during treatment. Because virus application and drying conditions had to be adapted to the absorbency and drying tolerance of each substrate, cross-substrate comparisons should be interpreted cautiously and mainly as indicators of material-dependent viral accessibility. The delayed inactivation of HAdV on plush fabric compared with paper and foam rubber suggests that the dense fibrous structure may partially shield virions from direct exposure to reactive species.
